🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Aristotle was a Greek thinker who lived about 2,350 years ago. He wanted to understand everything: animals, the stars, poems, governments, and why things move and change.

He asked a simple-sounding question: why? Why is a statue the way it is? He said there are four different kinds of answer. Take a bronze statue: it is made of bronze; it has the shape of a horse; a sculptor made it; and it was made to honor a winner of a race. Each is a different kind of "because".

blocks.name: gb-four-causes
blocks.cap: Pick a thing and see Aristotle's four kinds of "because" for it.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The four becauses game. Pick something in the room, like a chair. Ask four questions about it. What is it made of? What shape or plan does it follow? Who or what made it? What is it for? Try it with a bird's nest, a birthday cake and a tree.

Aristotle also thought heavy things fall faster than light things, in proportion to their weight. That sounds sensible: a stone drops faster than a leaf. About 1,900 years later, Galileo showed that if you take away the air, a heavy ball and a light ball fall together. Aristotle wasn't foolish. He was describing what we usually see in air and water. But he didn't test the rule carefully with balls of the same size.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Aristotle (384–322 BC) was born in Stagira in northern Greece, the son of a doctor. At seventeen he went to Athens and studied in Plato's Academy for about twenty years. After Plato died he lived on the island of Lesbos and elsewhere, tutored the young Alexander the Great for a few years, and in 335 BC returned to Athens and founded his own school, the Lyceum. The Physics is a set of lectures from his teaching, written down by him and edited by later scholars. "Physics" here means the study of physis, nature: everything that changes.

The problem he faced came from earlier thinkers. Parmenides had argued that change is impossible, since nothing can come from what is not. Zeno had offered puzzles "proving" that motion can't happen. Others, like Democritus, said everything is atoms bumping in a void, with no purpose. Aristotle wanted a science of change that accepted what our senses show: things really do move, grow and change.

head: Later name
The question it answers
For an oak tree
rows: What is it? What is its pattern?
a parent oak, through an acorn
What is it for? What is it heading toward?
a full-grown oak that makes acorns
blocks.cap: The Latin names come from Aristotle's medieval readers, not from Aristotle.

blocks.name: gb-four-causes
blocks.cap: The four causes for a statue, a house, an oak and a walk taken for health.

blocks.html: The final cause is the boldest. Aristotle saw purpose throughout nature: teeth grow sharp in front for biting, flat behind for grinding, and this, he argued, can't be mere luck because it happens always or for the most part. Modern biology explains such fit by natural selection instead (Darwin, 1859), but it still asks Aristotle's question: what is this part for?

blocks.text: Motion, the void and a surprise

blocks.html: Aristotle held that a thing moving through a medium like air or water goes faster when it is heavier and slower when the medium is thicker. In a void, with no medium at all, the speed would have to be infinite, which he took as absurd. So, he concluded, there is no void. In the middle of this argument he says something remarkable:

That is very close to Newton's first law, the law of inertia. But Aristotle meant it as an absurd consequence: if a void could exist, things in it would never stop, which he thought couldn't be. Newton, 2,000 years later, accepted exactly that conclusion.

blocks.name: gb-fall-rules
blocks.cap: Compare Aristotle's rule with what happens with no air and with real air, for two balls of the same size.

blocks.title: Aristotle's rule, worked out
blocks.q: By Aristotle's rule, speed is proportional to weight. A 2 kg stone falls a certain height in 6 seconds. How long would a 6 kg stone of the same shape take? What really happens?
steps: Three times the weight means three times the speed, so a third of the time: $6 \div 3 = 2$ seconds.
In fact, with little air resistance, both take about the same time. Dropped from 44 m, each takes about $\sqrt{2 \times 44 / 9.8} \approx 3$ seconds.
blocks.a: Aristotle's rule says 2 s; in reality both take nearly the same time.

blocks.html: Saying Aristotle never observed anything. He observed a great deal, and his rule fits motion through thick media fairly well: in water, a heavy pebble does sink faster than a light one of the same size, at a steady speed. The physicist Carlo Rovelli (2015) argued that Aristotle's physics is a fair approximation for objects moving through a fluid at their steady speed. What it misses is the case Galileo isolated: falling with the medium's effect taken away.

items: Time is the number of motion with respect to before and after (IV.11): time is how we count change.
The infinite exists only potentially: you can always divide a line again, but it is never divided into infinitely many pieces all at once.

Zeno's runner must first cover half the track, then half the rest, and so on. Aristotle answers that the time can be divided just as the distance can, so the runner crosses infinitely many "halves" in finite time. Mathematicians later showed that $\tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \dots = 1$.

blocks.title: Zeno's halves
blocks.q: A runner covers half of a 400 m track, then half of what is left, then half again, four times. How far has she gone, and how much is left?
steps: Left: $400 - 375 = 25$ m, the same as the last step. Each step leaves exactly as much as it covered.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Changed: the laws of motion. Galileo and Newton replaced Aristotle's rules with inertia and constant acceleration; the void he denied is real (Torricelli and Pascal made one in a tube of mercury).
Kept: careful definitions of motion, place, time and continuity; the potential infinite; and the habit of asking what causes change.
Debated still: whether there is purpose in nature. Physics dropped final causes; biology rephrased them; philosophers still argue about them.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Nature as a source of change

blocks.html: Aristotle defines a natural thing as one that has in itself "a source or cause of being moved and of being at rest" (II.1). A stone falls because of what it is; an acorn grows into an oak because of what it is. A bed, by contrast, changes only because someone makes or moves it. This contrast between nature and craft runs through the whole book.

Book VIII argues that motion has always existed and needs a first source that is itself unmoved, the unmoved mover. Medieval readers such as Aquinas (later on this ladder) used this argument in their own reasoning about God; Aristotle develops it further in the Metaphysics. Readers have long disagreed about how far the argument succeeds.

Aristotle's physics lasted nearly two thousand years because it fit everyday experience well. Things do stop when you stop pushing them; heavy things do usually fall faster in air. To get past it, Galileo had to imagine motion without friction or air, which nobody sees, and then test the idea with ramps and pendulums. Sometimes science moves forward by imagining what is not seen.

items: Is it a good argument to say "this happens always or for the most part, so it can't be chance"?
Aristotle rejected the void because it led to a strange conclusion. When should a strange conclusion make us reject an idea, and when should we accept it?
Can you think of a change that has no final cause? A change that seems to have one?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Play the four becauses game with something you made yourself. Which of the four causes is you?
  2. Drop a book and a sheet of paper together. Then crumple the paper into a ball and try again. What changed? What would Aristotle say?
  3. Aristotle said a thing in empty space would keep moving forever, and decided empty space can't exist. Newton said it does keep moving. Who seems right to you, and why?
  4. Is it fair to judge a thinker from long ago by what we know now?
  5. Zeno said a runner can never finish because there is always half the rest to run. What is wrong with his argument?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Some people think that long ago everyone believed the Earth was flat. That isn't so. Educated Greeks knew the Earth is a ball by the time of Aristotle, about 2,350 years ago, and he gave reasons you can check yourself.

His best reason: during an eclipse of the Moon, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, and the edge of the shadow is always curved. Only a ball casts a round shadow whichever way it is turned. A flat plate would sometimes cast a thin, straight shadow.

blocks.name: gb-earth-shadow
blocks.cap: Change the shape of the Earth and turn it. Which shape always casts a curved shadow?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Shadow test. In a dark room, shine a flashlight on a wall. Hold up a ball, then a paper plate, then a small box. Turn each one slowly. Which one always makes a round shadow? Now you know why Aristotle said the Earth is round.

Aristotle also noticed that when travelers go south, new stars appear above the southern horizon, stars that can't be seen from Greece. That only makes sense if the Earth's surface curves. But Aristotle also believed some things that turned out wrong: that the Earth sits still at the center of everything, and that the Sun, Moon and stars are carried around it on great invisible spheres.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Aristotle (384–322 BC) was born in Stagira in northern Greece, the son of a doctor. At seventeen he went to Athens and studied in Plato's Academy for about twenty years. After Plato died he lived on the island of Lesbos and elsewhere, tutored the young Alexander the Great for a few years, and in 335 BC returned to Athens and founded his own school, the Lyceum. On the Heavens is his account of the universe as a whole: the stars and planets, the Earth at the center, and the elements everything is made of.

The problem: earlier thinkers disagreed wildly about the cosmos. Some thought the Earth floated on water, or was a flat drum held up by air. The mathematician Eudoxus had built a model of nested spheres to explain the planets' motions. Aristotle wanted a physical account: what the heavens are made of, why they move in circles, and why the Earth is where it is and shaped as it is.

blocks.text: Two kinds of motion, five elements

items: Down and up: earth and water naturally move toward the center of the universe; air and fire naturally move away from it. Each element seeks its natural place.
Around: the heavens move in circles forever. So they must be made of a fifth element, which does not rise or fall, grow or decay. Later writers called it aether or the quintessence ("fifth essence").
The Earth sits at the center, at rest, because that is where all the heavy matter collects.

blocks.name: gb-earth-shadow
blocks.cap: A ball, a disk and a cube, each casting its shadow on the Moon. Turn them and slide the Moon into the shadow.

blocks.html: He adds that some stars seen in Egypt and Cyprus are never seen farther north, and reports that mathematicians had put the Earth's circumference at 400,000 stades. That is the oldest estimate of the Earth's size we have. A stade was a racecourse length, and Greek stades varied, so we can't convert it exactly; on most estimates it is about one and a half to two times the true size.

blocks.title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
blocks.q: About a century after Aristotle, Eratosthenes found that at noon on midsummer day the Sun was straight overhead at Syene but 7.2° from overhead at Alexandria, which he took to be 5,000 stades north. What circumference does this give?
steps: A full circle is 360°, and $360 \div 7.2 = 50$.
So the distance from Syene to Alexandria is $\tfrac{1}{50}$ of the way round.
Circumference $= 50 \times 5000 = 250{,}000$ stades.

blocks.name: gb-fall-rules
blocks.cap: Aristotle's rule against falling with no air and in real air.

blocks.html: Believing the story that Galileo dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to refute this passage in front of a crowd. The story comes from Galileo's student Viviani, written years later, and Galileo's own writings don't describe it; historians doubt it happened as told. Galileo's real evidence came from rolling balls down ramps and from careful argument. Others, such as Simon Stevin in 1586, had already dropped unequal lead balls and seen them land together.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the spherical Earth and the evidence for it, which every astronomer since has accepted.

Changed: the unchanging heavens. Tycho Brahe showed in 1572 and 1577 that a new star and a comet were far beyond the Moon. Galileo's telescope (1610) found mountains on the Moon and moons around Jupiter.
Changed: the Earth at rest in the center. Copernicus (1543) put the Sun at the center, and Newton showed that the same gravity rules the heavens and the Earth, ending Aristotle's split between them.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Why a different physics for the sky?

blocks.html: On Earth things start and stop, rise and fall, are born and decay. In the sky, as far as any Greek could see, the stars kept the same patterns forever and moved in perfect circles. Aristotle concluded that the heavens are made of different stuff with different laws. It was a reasonable inference from the evidence of his day, and it was the main idea that Galileo and Newton overturned.

Aristotle's model put each planet on a set of nested spheres, following Eudoxus and Callippus, 55 spheres in all. It could not explain why planets change in brightness, which suggested their distance changes. Later astronomers, above all Ptolemy (next on this ladder), used other circles instead, while keeping Aristotle's Earth at rest in the center.

items: Aristotle reasoned from evidence and got some things right and some wrong. What would have helped him tell which was which?
Why might people prefer to believe that the heavens are perfect and unchanging?
Many people today think medieval people believed in a flat Earth. Why do myths about the past spread?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Try the shadow test with a ball and a plate. How would you explain Aristotle's argument to a friend?
  2. Have you seen a lunar eclipse? If one comes up, watch the edge of the shadow together.
  3. Why might sailors have been some of the first people to suspect the Earth is curved? (Think about ships coming over the horizon.)
  4. Aristotle thought the sky was made of a different element from the Earth. What would it take to change your mind about something everyone around you believes?
  5. Is it surprising that a thinker could be right about the shape of the Earth and wrong about whether it moves?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Aristotle describes dissection and animal breeding plainly. The lesson keeps to observation and classification.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Aristotle loved animals. While living on the Greek island of Lesbos, he studied the sea creatures of a big lagoon there: fish, octopus, crabs, sea urchins. He asked fishermen, farmers and beekeepers what they knew, and he cut animals open to see how they were made inside.

He described about five hundred kinds of animals. He noticed that a dolphin breathes air and feeds its babies milk, like a cow, even though it lives in the sea and looks like a fish. Many people after him called dolphins and whales fish. Aristotle had already seen the difference.

blocks.name: gb-animal-tree
blocks.cap: Pick an animal to see where Aristotle put it, and what scientists say today.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Watch like Aristotle. Choose one small animal you can watch safely without touching it: an ant, a bird at a feeder, a snail after rain, a pet. Watch for ten minutes and write down everything it does. How does it move? What does it eat? Draw it. Next time, see if you notice something new.

Aristotle also watched a chicken grow inside its egg. He opened eggs day after day and saw that after about three days a tiny red speck appears, beating: the chick's heart. Scientists still study chick eggs this way.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Aristotle (384–322 BC) was born in Stagira in northern Greece, the son of a doctor. At seventeen he went to Athens and studied in Plato's Academy for about twenty years. After Plato died he lived on the island of Lesbos and elsewhere, tutored the young Alexander the Great for a few years, and in 335 BC returned to Athens and founded his own school, the Lyceum. Much of his work on animals seems to come from his years on Lesbos (c. 345–343 BC) with his student Theophrastus, who went on to write the first great books on plants. Many of his sea creatures can be identified with those of the island's lagoon at Pyrrha.

Before Aristotle, Greek writing about animals was mostly fable, medicine or farming advice. Nobody had tried to describe all the kinds of animals and explain why their bodies are built as they are. The animal books are about a quarter of his surviving writings.

head: Work
What it does
rows: collects facts: parts, ways of life, food, breeding and behavior of hundreds of animals ("history" here means inquiry)
explains why animals have the parts they do, chiefly by what each part is for
Motion of Animals and Gait of Animals
how animals move: legs, wings, fins, and the reason for walking on four, two or many legs

blocks.html: Modern embryology agrees closely: a chick's heart begins to beat in the second day of incubation and is easy to see by the third. Aristotle also described the octopus's special mating arm, and how a kind of dogfish nourishes its young through a cord like a mammal's. Both reports were doubted for centuries and confirmed in the 1800s.

blocks.name: gb-animal-tree
blocks.cap: Aristotle's main groups, with what biologists say now.

blocks.html: Aristotle did not build a single tree like modern biologists. He sorted animals by many features at once: blood or no blood, live birth or eggs, lungs or gills, how they move. His main split, animals with red blood and without, matches our split between vertebrates and invertebrates almost exactly. Among the bloodless animals he separated the soft-bodied cephalopods, the crustaceans, the shelled animals and the insects, groups biologists still recognize.

blocks.title: Sort by two features
blocks.q: Aristotle noticed that animals with lungs and live birth include land animals and some sea animals. Of these five, which have red blood and bear live young: horse, dolphin, eagle, octopus, bat?
steps: Red blood: horse, dolphin, eagle, bat. The octopus has none (its blood is blue).
Live young: horse, dolphin, bat. The eagle lays eggs.

blocks.html: Assuming Aristotle got everything right because he got so much right. He thought the heart, not the brain, was the seat of thought and feeling, and that the brain cooled the blood. He wrote that men have more teeth than women, which a count would have corrected. He also repeated some fishermen's and travelers' tales without checking them. Like all observers, he was right where he looked carefully and wrong where he trusted reports or theory.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: many of his observations, his main groups of animals, and the method of comparing the same part across many animals (comparative anatomy).
Changed: Aristotle thought each kind of animal is fixed forever. Darwin (1859) showed that species change and share common ancestors, which explains why their parts fit their ways of life.
Admired: after reading Ogle's translation of Parts of Animals in 1882, Darwin wrote to Ogle that Linnaeus and Cuvier had been his "two gods", but "they were mere school-boys to old Aristotle".

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Why are animals built as they are?

blocks.html: Parts of Animals explains features chiefly by their purpose: birds have beaks of different shapes for different foods, animals with horns do not also have tusks, because nature does not give double defenses. Aristotle also recognized "necessity": some features are simply the result of what bodies are made of. This mix of purpose and necessity is still how biologists think, though Darwin changed what "purpose" means: a part is "for" something because ancestors with that part left more offspring.

Aristotle also saw a "ladder of nature" running from plants up to people, with no sharp breaks: sponges and sea anemones, he said, are hard to place as plant or animal. Later writers made this into a rigid ranking; Aristotle treated it as a gradual series. Modern biology replaces the ladder with a branching tree.

items: Is the dolphin's resemblance to a fish or to a cow more important? How do you decide which features matter for sorting?
Aristotle trusted fishermen's reports. When should a scientist trust other people's observations?
Why might studying "humble" animals, like worms or snails, be as important as studying lions?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Do the ten-minute animal watch. What surprised you?
  2. Is a dolphin more like a fish or more like a cow? What makes you say so?
  3. Aristotle thought some of his ideas were right because they seemed sensible, like the heart doing our thinking. How could he have tested that?
  4. Why do you think Aristotle said even humble animals are worth studying?
  5. Make your own way to sort ten animals. Do you sort by where they live, what they eat or how they're built? What changes?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The Hippocratic books describe illness and injury frankly, and the Epidemics record many deaths. The lesson keeps to the ideas; the young readers' path has no medical detail.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Long ago, when people got sick, many thought an angry god had sent the illness. About 2,400 years ago, on the Greek island of Cos, a doctor named Hippocrates and the doctors who learned from him said something new: illness has natural causes, like food, weather, water and the way people live. If you watch carefully, you can learn those causes.

These doctors wrote down what they saw, day by day, for each sick person they visited: the fever, the sleep, the breathing, whether the person got better. Their notes are some of the oldest doctors' records in the world.
Watch carefully, write down what you see, and look for natural causes. That is the Hippocratic way.

🧩 Try this

Be a weather watcher, like the Hippocratic doctors. For one week, write down each morning: Is it warm or cold? Wet or dry? Windy? Which way is the wind blowing? At the end of the week, look at your notes. Did anything happen more on some kinds of days than others? (Maybe your dog was sleepier on rainy days, or the laundry took longer to dry.) You have just made a small study, the way they did.

Young doctors today often still make a promise when they finish their training. The oldest promise of this kind is the Hippocratic Oath: to help the sick as well as they can, to keep their secrets, and never to use their skill to hurt anyone.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460–c. 370 BC) was a famous physician in the time of Socrates. Plato mentions him as a well-known doctor who taught medicine for a fee. Almost everything else told about his life comes from biographies written centuries later.

The books under his name, the Hippocratic Corpus, are about sixty works written by many authors, mostly between about 430 and 350 BC, with some later. They disagree with one another in places. Which of them, if any, Hippocrates wrote himself is unknown. When we say "Hippocrates says", we mean "a writer in the Hippocratic Corpus says".

The problem these writers faced was how to make medicine a craft that could be learned and trusted. Around them were healers who blamed gods or spirits, and philosophers who explained the body from a single principle such as heat or water. The Hippocratic writers wanted medicine built on what can be observed in patients.

blocks.text: A disease with a natural cause

blocks.html: The "sacred disease" is epilepsy. The writer argues that it has the same kind of cause as other diseases, and places that cause in the brain. He also criticizes healers who claimed to cure it with charms and purifications. Modern medicine agrees that epilepsy is a condition of the brain, though not with his explanation of how it arises.

On Airs, Waters, and Places tells a traveling doctor to study a new town before treating anyone: which way it faces, its winds, its water and how its people live. It is one of the first works to link health with environment, an idea at the heart of modern public health.

The Epidemics record what happened to particular patients, day by day, named by where they lived: their fevers, sleep, thirst and recovery or death. Many of the patients died; the writers recorded failures as well as successes. The Prognostics teach how to foresee the course of an illness from signs, so the doctor can tell the family what to expect.

Saying the Hippocratic Oath contains the words "First, do no harm". It doesn't. The Latin slogan primum non nocere appears only in the 1800s. The nearest ancient words are in the Epidemics, quoted above: "to do good or to do no harm". The Oath itself promises to use treatment to help the sick and to keep them from harm and injustice.

The Oath is a short text in which a new physician swears by the gods of healing to honor his teacher, to teach medicine to his teacher's sons and to his own pupils, to treat the sick for their benefit, never to give a deadly drug, to keep secret what he sees and hears, and to live a pure life. Medical schools today use many rewritten versions, and people disagree about some of its old promises and how they apply now. The original Oath was a pledge for one group of Greek doctors; it was never a law.

blocks.name: gb-qualities
blocks.cap: Pick a humor to see its qualities, element and season. This is a historical theory, not modern medicine.

blocks.html: One Hippocratic work, On the Nature of Man (not in the Great Books selection; Aristotle says it was by Polybus, Hippocrates' son-in-law), says the body contains four humors, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, and that health is their right mixture. Galen made this theory central, and it ruled Western and Islamic medicine until the 1800s. Not every Hippocratic writer agreed: On Ancient Medicine attacks doctors who reduce the body to hot, cold, wet and dry.

blocks.text: What later medicine kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: looking for natural causes; careful case records; prognosis; the link between environment and health; confidentiality and the duty to the patient.

Changed: the humors were abandoned. Cell theory (Virchow, 1858) and germ theory (Pasteur and Koch, 1860s–1880s) explained disease in new ways, and treatments built on the humors, such as bleeding patients, were given up.
Still debated: how the old ideals of the Oath apply to new questions in medicine.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

On Ancient Medicine argues that medicine is an old craft, discovered by long trial, like cooking: people found which foods made them strong and which made them ill. It warns against new theories that start from an assumed principle, such as "the hot", and deduce everything else. Philosophers, the writer says, should learn from medicine about human nature, not the other way round. This is one of the earliest arguments for experience over theory, and it anticipates Bacon's attack, much later on this ladder, on reasoning that runs ahead of observation.

Yet the same collection also contains bold theory, such as the four humors. The Hippocratic Corpus is less a single doctrine than a long argument among doctors about how medicine should be done. Reading two of its works side by side shows that argument.

items: What should a doctor do when they do not know what will help? "At least do no harm" sounds simple; when is it hard?
Why would a writer 2,400 years ago record cases where the patient died? What does that tell you about his aims?
Is a promise like the Oath still useful when the old version has been rewritten many times?

blocks.html: Galen, later on this ladder, took Hippocrates as his hero and built a whole system on him. Harvey's discovery of the circulation of the blood, much later, began the end of that system.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. People once thought some illnesses were sent by gods. Why might it be hard to change a belief like that?
  2. The Hippocratic doctors studied a town's winds and water. What about where you live might affect people's health?
  3. Doctors promise to keep patients' secrets. Why is that important?
  4. "Life is short, and the Art long." What do you think it means? Is it true of anything you are learning?
  5. If you were writing a promise for doctors today, what would you put in it?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

About 2,300 years ago, in the city of Alexandria in Egypt, a teacher named Euclid wrote a book about shapes. He started with a few things everyone agrees on, like you can draw a straight line from any point to any other point. Then, step by step, he proved hundreds of new facts. Each step used only the facts before it.

His book, the Elements, was used to teach geometry for more than 2,000 years. Some people say it has been copied and printed more than any other book except the Bible. Nobody can count that for sure, but it was the main math book in schools for a very long time.
A proof is a chain of reasons. Each link must hold, and nothing can be taken on trust except the few starting rules Euclid wrote down at the beginning.

blocks.name: gb-euclid-i1
blocks.cap: Euclid's very first proof: how to make a triangle with three equal sides using only a straightedge and a compass. Press Next step.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Make Euclid's triangle with string. You need two pencils, a piece of string and paper. Draw a line AB. Tie the string to a pencil and hold the other end on A, so the string reaches exactly to B. Swing a circle. Do the same from B. Where the two circles cross, mark C. Join C to A and to B. Measure the three sides. Why must they be equal?

Euclid's most famous proof is near the end of his first book. If a triangle has a square corner, the squares built on its two short sides add up to the square on its long side. A 3, 4, 5 triangle works: 9 + 16 = 25. Builders have used that trick to make square corners for a very long time.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Euclid taught in Alexandria around 300 BC, in the years after Alexander the Great, when the new Greek kings of Egypt were filling the city with scholars. We know almost nothing else about his life. Later writers tell a few stories, but they wrote centuries afterward.

The problem Euclid faced was not a lack of geometry. Greek mathematicians had found a great many results over the previous 250 years, and Egyptian and Babylonian scribes had used practical rules for far longer. The problem was order. Which facts depend on which? What do you have to assume? Euclid gathered the known results into one chain, starting from a small set of definitions, postulates and common notions, and proved everything else from them.

The axiomatic method. State your definitions and assumptions at the start. Then accept nothing else without proof. Each proposition may use only the starting points and the propositions already proved.

Postulates 1 to 3 describe the two tools allowed: a straightedge (to draw and extend lines) and a compass (to draw circles). The fifth, the parallel postulate, is longer and less obvious than the rest. Euclid held it back until Proposition 29, as if he used it only when he had to.

blocks.name: gb-euclid-i1
blocks.cap: Drag A or B, then step through the construction. Each step names the postulate or definition it rests on.

blocks.html: Notice the pattern every proposition follows: a statement of what is to be done or proved, a figure with lettered points, the construction, the proof with a reason for each step, and the closing words: being what it was required to do (for a construction) or what it was required to prove (for a theorem). Later readers shortened the Latin form of the second to Q.E.D.

blocks.text: What Books I to IV contain

head: Book
Subject
A landmark
rows: I.32: the angles of a triangle make two right angles; I.47: the Pythagorean theorem
II.4: the square on a whole line equals the squares on its two parts plus twice the rectangle on them, our $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$
III.31: an angle in a semicircle is right
Polygons drawn in and around circles
IV.11: the regular pentagon; IV.16: the regular 15-sided figure
blocks.cap: Books I to IV are the plane geometry most schools still teach.

blocks.text: The theorem at the end of Book I

blocks.html: Euclid means real squares with real areas, not numbers. His proof draws a line from the right angle straight down through the big square, cutting it into two rectangles, and shows that each rectangle has the same area as one of the small squares. The visual below shows the same equality by sliding the squares, using two facts Euclid proves earlier: parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area (I.35), and a triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height (I.41).

blocks.name: gb-euclid-i47
blocks.cap: Drag the corner A around the half circle, then play the three moves. Each move keeps the area the same.

blocks.title: A ladder and a wall
blocks.q: A ladder 13 feet long leans against a wall with its foot 5 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The wall and the ground make a right angle, so the ladder is the side opposite the right angle.

blocks.title: The third angle
blocks.q: Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 71°. What is the third, and what is the exterior angle beside it?
steps: By I.32 the three angles make two right angles: 180°.
The third angle is $180 - 48 - 71 = 61$ degrees.
The exterior angle next to it is $180 - 61 = 119$ degrees, which is also $48 + 71$, the two opposite interior angles (also I.32).

blocks.html: Thinking Euclid invented all of this. The Pythagorean theorem was known long before Pythagoras: a Babylonian clay tablet from about 1800 BC (Plimpton 322) lists sets of numbers like 3, 4, 5 that fit it. Euclid's own contribution was the order and the proofs. Another slip: "Q.E.D." is not in Euclid. It is the Latin shortening, used by later editors, of his closing Greek phrase.

blocks.text: What later mathematics kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: almost every result in Books I to IV, the idea of proof from stated assumptions, and the compass-and-straightedge constructions still taught in school.
Repaired: Euclid sometimes relied on a figure. In I.1 he never proves that the two circles actually cross. In 1899 David Hilbert rewrote the foundations with a longer, complete list of axioms.

Changed: in the 1820s and 1830s Nikolai Lobachevsky and János Bolyai showed that a consistent geometry can be built with the parallel postulate replaced (Gauss had reached the same idea privately). Einstein's general relativity (1915) describes space-time with such curved geometry.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

For two thousand years mathematicians tried to prove the parallel postulate from the other four, Ptolemy and Proclus among them, and later Islamic mathematicians such as Omar Khayyam and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, and the Italian Girolamo Saccheri (1733). Each attempt either failed or quietly assumed something equal to it. The eventual answer was surprising: it can't be proved, because geometries where it is false are just as consistent.

This changed how mathematicians think about axioms. They are no longer "self-evident truths" about space but chosen starting points. Which geometry describes the real world is a question for measurement, not for logic alone.

No copy from Euclid's time survives. Our text comes from medieval Greek manuscripts (the oldest dated one, at Oxford, was copied in AD 888), from Arabic translations made in Baghdad around AD 800, and from Latin translations made from the Arabic and the Greek in the 1100s. Small papyrus scraps from Roman Egypt show that the text was much the same in about AD 100. The first printed edition came out in Venice in 1482. The standard Greek text today is J. L. Heiberg's (1883–1888), which Heath translated.

Readers have argued about the story that King Ptolemy asked Euclid for an easier way and was told there is "no royal road" to geometry. It comes from Proclus, writing about 750 years later, and a nearly identical story is told of another mathematician and Alexander the Great. Treat it as a legend about the subject, not a fact about the man.

items: Is a proof that relies on a picture really a proof?
Why does a list of five postulates produce so much? Could a different list produce a different world?
Many people, from Abraham Lincoln to Bertrand Russell, said studying Euclid taught them what it means to prove something. What does a proof give you that a measurement can't?

blocks.html: Later books on this ladder answer Euclid directly. Spinoza wrote his Ethics in Euclid's form, with definitions, axioms and propositions. Descartes joined geometry to algebra. Newton set out the Principia as propositions with proofs, in Euclid's manner.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Euclid accepted five postulates without proof. What would you put on a list of things "everyone agrees on" about shapes?
  2. Why do you think Euclid's book was used in schools for so long? Is there any book you think will still be read in 2,000 years?
  3. Is it enough to measure a few right triangles and see that the squares add up? What does Euclid's proof give you that measuring doesn't?
  4. The parallel postulate turned out not to be necessary. Can you think of a rule that seemed obvious to you but turned out not to be true everywhere?
  5. Try the string construction together. What could go wrong if the string stretched?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
In the middle of his book, Euclid stops drawing triangles and starts thinking about numbers. He asks questions you can explore with counters or blocks.

Some numbers can be made into a rectangle of dots in more than one way: 12 dots can be 3 rows of 4, or 2 rows of 6. Others, like 7 or 13, only make a single row. Those are the prime numbers. Euclid proved something amazing about them: they never run out. However many primes you list, there is always another.
Euclid's trick for finding a new prime: multiply all the primes on your list and add 1. The answer can't be divided evenly by any prime on your list, so its prime factors are new ones.

🧩 Try this

Try it. Start with the primes 2, 3 and 5. Multiply: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. Add 1: 31. Try dividing 31 by 2, 3 and 5. There is always 1 left over! (31 happens to be prime itself.) Now try 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30,031. It isn't prime: 30,031 = 59 × 509. But 59 and 509 are new primes, not on the list. Euclid's argument works either way.

blocks.name: gb-euclid-gcd
blocks.cap: Euclid's way to find the biggest number that measures two others: keep cutting the biggest squares you can out of a rectangle. Press Cut.

blocks.html: Euclid also found perfect numbers: numbers equal to the sum of their smaller divisors. 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 is the first. 28 = 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 is the next.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Books V to X of the Elements (Euclid, Alexandria, c. 300 BC) tackle a crisis in Greek mathematics. The Pythagoreans had hoped that everything could be measured by whole numbers. Then someone discovered that the diagonal of a square and its side have no common measure: no unit, however small, fits a whole number of times into both. Their ratio is what we call $\sqrt{2}$, and it is not a ratio of whole numbers.

If lengths can't always be compared as numbers, how can geometry use ratios at all? Book V gives the answer, a theory of proportion credited by ancient writers to Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–c. 340 BC). It defines when two ratios are equal without needing them to be ratios of whole numbers. Book VI then applies it to similar figures.

head: Book
Subject
A landmark
rows: Ratio and proportion for any magnitudes
Definition 5: when ratios are "in the same ratio" (Eudoxus)
VI.2: a line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides proportionally
IX.20: there are infinitely many primes; IX.36: how to make perfect numbers
a long classification of lines like $\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}$; X.1 is a first step toward limits

blocks.html: Book VII, Proposition 2 shows how to find the greatest common measure of two numbers: subtract the smaller from the larger again and again (or, as we say now, divide and keep the remainder) until the remainder measures the number before it. If the process ends at the unit, the numbers are prime to one another (VII.1). It is one of the oldest procedures still in daily use: computers run it to reduce fractions and in the arithmetic behind encryption.

blocks.name: gb-euclid-gcd
blocks.cap: Choose a length and width, then cut. The side of the last square is the greatest common measure.

blocks.title: A greatest common measure
blocks.q: Find the greatest common measure of 1,071 and 462 by Euclid's method.
steps: The last nonzero remainder, 21, measures both numbers. No larger number does.

blocks.html: Euclid's proof takes three primes A, B and C, multiplies them and adds the unit. The new number is either prime itself, or it has a prime factor, and that factor can't be A, B or C, because each of those leaves a remainder of 1. Either way there is a prime not on the list. The same argument works for a list of any length. Notice how careful he is: he does not say "infinitely many", a phrase Greek mathematicians avoided. He says that for any list, there are more.

Thinking that $2 \times 3 \times 5 \times \dots \times p + 1$ is always prime. It isn't: $2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11 \times 13 + 1 = 30{,}031 = 59 \times 509$. Euclid never claimed it was. He only needs it to have a prime factor that is not on the list.

blocks.title: Euclid's recipe
blocks.q: Use IX.36 to find the third perfect number.
steps: Double from the unit and add as you go: 1 + 2 = 3 (prime), 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 (prime), 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 (not prime), 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 (prime).
The first two primes give $3 \times 2 = 6$ and $7 \times 4 = 28$.
The next prime sum, 31, times the last number added, 16, gives $31 \times 16 = 496$.
Check: the parts of 496 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 62, 124, 248, which add to 496.

blocks.text: What later mathematics kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the Euclidean algorithm, the infinitude of primes and IX.36 are all still taught, with the same proofs.
Finished: in the 1700s Leonhard Euler proved the converse for even numbers: every even perfect number comes from Euclid's recipe. Whether any odd perfect number exists is still unknown.

Changed: Eudoxus's theory of proportion was rebuilt in 1872 by Richard Dedekind, whose definition of the real numbers follows Book V's Definition 5 closely. Today we treat $\sqrt{2}$ as a number; Euclid treated it as a ratio of lines.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Euclid keeps two worlds apart. Numbers (Books VII–IX) are collections of units: 1 is not even a number for him, just the unit. Magnitudes (Books V, VI, X) are lengths, areas and volumes, which can be divided without end. The discovery of incommensurables is why: some magnitudes simply are not counts of a common unit. Much of the history of mathematics from Descartes to Dedekind is the story of joining the two worlds back together into one number line.

Book X, the longest in the Elements, sorts 13 kinds of irrational lines. Its first proposition, that halving again and again eventually leaves something smaller than any given magnitude, is the basis of the "method of exhaustion" used in Book XII and by Archimedes, an ancestor of the limits of calculus.

items: Are numbers discovered or invented? Euclid's primes were there before anyone counted them, weren't they?
Why should a proof that something exists (another prime) be satisfying even when it doesn't hand you the thing?
Euclid's algorithm is 2,300 years old and is now part of the arithmetic of computer encryption. What other old ideas have found new uses?

blocks.html: Nicomachus, later on this ladder, covers much of the same number lore as Books VII–IX but without proofs, by listing examples. Comparing the two shows the difference between knowing that something is true and knowing why.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Euclid proved the primes never run out, without listing them all. How can you know something about a list you can never finish?
  2. Try Euclid's "multiply and add 1" trick on 2 and 3, then on 2, 3, 5 and 7. What do you get each time?
  3. Why might the discovery that the diagonal and side of a square have no common measure have upset people who believed "all is number"?
  4. Perfect numbers have no practical use that anyone knows of, yet people have hunted them for 2,000 years. Why do people study things that have no use?
  5. Is there a difference between knowing that something is true and knowing why? Give an example from everyday life.

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

At the very end of his book, Euclid builds shapes you can hold. A regular solid is a solid whose faces are all the same regular shape, with the same number meeting at every corner. A cube is one: six square faces, three at every corner.
How many regular solids are there? You might guess there are as many as you like. Euclid proved there are exactly five, and showed how to build each one.

blocks.name: gb-platonic
blocks.cap: The five regular solids. Drag to turn them.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Why only five? Cut out paper triangles with three equal sides. Tape 3 around a point and fold them up: a corner of a pyramid. 4 works too (an octahedron), and 5 (an icosahedron). Try 6: they lie flat! Six triangles make 360°, a full turn, so there is nothing to fold. Now try squares (3 works, 4 lies flat) and pentagons (3 works). Hexagons? Three of them already lie flat. That is Euclid's argument.
Euclid also measured shapes. He proved that a cone holds exactly a third of a cylinder with the same base and height. You can test it with a paper cone, a paper tube and some rice.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Books XI to XIII finish the Elements (Euclid, Alexandria, c. 300 BC) by moving into three dimensions. Book XI sets up solid geometry: lines and planes in space, solid angles, and boxes. Book XII measures curved and pointed solids. Book XIII constructs the five regular solids inside a sphere and proves there are no others.

Why end there? The five regular solids were famous: Plato's dialogue Timaeus (c. 360 BC) had matched four of them to earth, air, fire and water, and the fifth to the whole cosmos. Euclid's own interest is mathematical. Book XIII uses almost everything before it: proportion, the golden section ("extreme and mean ratio", from Book VI), and the irrational lines of Book X. Many readers see it as the summit the whole work climbs toward, though that is a reading, not something Euclid says.

How do you prove a pyramid is a third of a prism without calculus? Book XII uses the method of exhaustion, credited to Eudoxus. Fill the shape with simpler pieces you can measure, then show that the leftover can be made smaller than any amount you name. Then prove, by a double argument, that the answer can be neither more nor less than claimed. Archimedes pushed the method much further.

Book XII's results, in modern form: circles are to one another as the squares on their diameters (XII.2); a pyramid is a third of the prism with the same base and height (XII.7); a cone is a third of the cylinder (XII.10); spheres are to one another as the cubes of their diameters (XII.18).

blocks.title: A cone a third of a cylinder
blocks.q: A cylinder of ice cream has a base of area 30 square centimeters and a height of 12 centimeters. How much does a cone with the same base and height hold?
steps: The cylinder holds base × height = $30 \times 12 = 360$ cubic centimeters.
By XII.10 the cone is a third of that: $360 \div 3 = 120$.

blocks.title: Spheres by their diameters
blocks.q: One ball is three times as wide as another. How many times as much does it hold?
steps: By XII.18 spheres are to one another as the cubes of their diameters.

blocks.name: gb-platonic
blocks.cap: Pick a solid. The readout counts faces, edges and corners and adds up the angles at one corner.

blocks.html: After the last construction, Euclid adds a short argument that no other regular solid exists. At each corner at least three faces must meet, and the angles at the corner must add up to less than four right angles (360°), or the faces lie flat. Equilateral triangles have 60° corners, so 3, 4 or 5 of them fit (180°, 240°, 300°). Squares have 90°, so only 3 (270°). Regular pentagons have 108°, so only 3 (324°). Hexagons have 120°, and three already make 360°. Nothing larger fits at all.

head: Solid
Faces
Meeting at each corner
Faces
Edges
Corners
blocks.cap: In every row, corners − edges + faces = 2. Euclid did not notice this; Descartes came close and Euler stated it in 1750.

blocks.html: Calling them "Plato's solids" as if Plato discovered them. Ancient sources credit Pythagoreans with some and Theaetetus (c. 417–369 BC) with the octahedron and icosahedron and the first general treatment; Plato wrote about them, and Euclid gave the complete constructions and the proof that there are only five.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the volume results of Book XII and the five-solid theorem, both exactly right.
Changed: Kepler, early in his career, tried to fit the planets' orbits between nested regular solids (1596). The idea was wrong, but the search led him to his real laws of planetary motion.
Found in nature: some viruses and many minerals have the symmetry of these solids; table salt forms cubes, and many virus shells are icosahedral.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Exhaustion proofs are rigorous but slow: you must already know the answer, then prove that nothing else is possible. Archimedes, Cavalieri, Fermat and finally Newton and Leibniz looked for a method that finds the answer, not just checks it. The integral of calculus is the descendant of Book XII.

Euler's formula, $V - E + F = 2$, holds for every solid without holes, regular or not. It was one of the first results of topology, the geometry of shapes that can be stretched. Euclid's careful counts of faces and edges contain it, though he never wrote it down.

items: Why might the fact that there are exactly five regular solids, no more, have seemed to Plato and Kepler to say something about the universe itself?
Is a beautiful idea more likely to be true? Kepler's nested solids were beautiful and wrong; his ellipses seemed less beautiful and were right.
What is the difference between filling a shape with smaller and smaller pieces forever, and actually finishing?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Build the five solids from paper or with toothpicks and clay. Which is hardest? Count the faces, edges and corners of each.
  2. Why can't six equilateral triangles meet at the corner of a solid?
  3. Dice for games come in all five shapes. Why would a game maker want a regular solid for a die?
  4. Plato thought the five solids were the shapes of the elements. Kepler thought they spaced the planets. Why do people look for simple patterns in nature, and when does that go wrong?
  5. A cone holds a third of a cylinder. How could you test that at home?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Archimedes lived in Syracuse, a Greek city on the island of Sicily, about 2,250 years ago. He was a mathematician who loved to measure things nobody else could: the space inside a ball, the number of grains of sand it would take to fill the whole sky, and the reason a ship floats.

He worked out the rule of the lever. A small weight far from the balance point can lift a big weight close to it. That is why a long crowbar can move a heavy rock, and why a small child at the far end of a seesaw can balance a grown-up sitting near the middle.

blocks.name: gb-lever
blocks.cap: Change the weights and distances. When weight × distance is the same on both sides, the beam balances.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A ruler seesaw. Balance a ruler on a pencil at its middle mark. Put 2 coins at the 3 cm mark on one side. Where must 1 coin go on the other side to balance? (Try 6 cm.) Now try 3 coins at 2 cm. Can you predict the answer before you test it?

There is a famous story that Archimedes jumped out of his bath shouting "Eureka!" ("I have found it!") when he saw how to test whether a king's crown was pure gold. The story was written down about 200 years after he died, by a Roman builder named Vitruvius, so nobody knows whether it happened. But the science is real: water pushes up on anything in it, and a crown with cheap silver mixed in takes up more room than pure gold of the same weight.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Archimedes (c. 287–212 BC) lived in Syracuse when it was a wealthy Greek city allied with Rome. He corresponded with mathematicians at Alexandria, sending them his results with letters that open many of his books. He died when Roman forces captured Syracuse during the Second Punic War. Plutarch, writing about 300 years later, gives several versions of how a Roman soldier killed him, and says the Roman general Marcellus was grieved by it.

His problem was measurement. Euclid had shown how to prove things about shapes, but many questions stayed open. How do you find the area of a curved shape, or the volume of a sphere? Why does a lever work? What makes some things float? Archimedes answered them with proofs as careful as Euclid's, often in short books addressed to friends.
On the Equilibrium of Planes starts from a few postulates, like "equal weights at equal distances balance", and proves the law of the lever as a theorem.
Reciprocally proportional means the bigger weight sits at the smaller distance, in the same ratio: if $W_1 : W_2 = d_2 : d_1$, the lever balances. In modern words, $W_1 d_1 = W_2 d_2$.

blocks.name: gb-lever
blocks.cap: Set any weights and distances on the notches. The readout multiplies weight by distance on each side.

blocks.title: Lifting a stone
blocks.q: A stone weighing 600 newtons sits 0.3 m from the pivot of a crowbar. How hard must you push down 1.8 m from the pivot on the other side to balance it?
steps: Weight × distance must match: $600 \times 0.3 = F \times 1.8$.
A push of a sixth of the weight, because the arm is six times as long.

blocks.html: Pappus of Alexandria, five centuries later, reports Archimedes saying, in effect, give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth. The words are a later report, but the idea is exactly the law of the lever: with a long enough arm, any weight can be balanced.

Proposition 5 deals with floating: a floating solid sinks until it has pushed aside its own weight of fluid. Together they give Archimedes' principle: anything in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside. A floating ship sinks until it has pushed aside its own weight of water. A stone is pushed up too, just not enough to float.

blocks.name: gb-crown
blocks.cap: Mix some silver into the crown, then lower both into water. The crown and the gold weigh the same in air; in water the bulkier one is pushed up more.

blocks.title: Weighing a crown in water
blocks.q: A crown weighs 1,000 g in air and 940 g when hanging in water. Pure gold is about 19.3 times as dense as water. Is it pure gold?
steps: In water it lost 60 g, so it pushed aside 60 g of water: its volume is 60 cm³.
Its density is $1000 \div 60 \approx 16.7$ times water.
Pure gold would be 19.3, losing only $1000 \div 19.3 \approx 52$ g. The crown is too bulky for its weight.
blocks.a: No: its density is about 16.7, less than gold's 19.3, so something lighter is mixed in.

blocks.html: Believing the bathtub story as told. Vitruvius (writing about 25 BC) says Archimedes measured the water each object spilled over. Galileo, in a short essay of 1586 called La Bilancetta ("the little balance"), argued that the spilled water would be too small to measure well, and suggested Archimedes more likely weighed the crown and gold in water on a balance, using his own principle. Whether the crown story happened at all is unknown.

Archimedes drew regular polygons inside and outside a circle, starting with hexagons and doubling the sides four times, to 96. The circle's perimeter is caught between the two polygons. He had no decimals and no algebra; he worked with whole-number fractions and careful estimates of square roots, rounding in the safe direction each time.

blocks.name: gb-circle-pi
blocks.cap: Double the sides and watch the two polygons squeeze the circle.

blocks.title: The first step
blocks.q: Find Archimedes' bounds from hexagons alone, for a circle of diameter 1.
steps: The inside hexagon has six sides, each equal to the radius, $\tfrac12$. Its perimeter is 3.
The outside hexagon has sides $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.5774$. Its perimeter is $6 \times 0.5774 \approx 3.464$.
So $3 < \pi < 3.464$. Doubling to 96 sides narrows this to between about 3.1410 and 3.1427, which Archimedes rounded, always in the safe direction, to 3 10/71 and 3 1/7.

items: On the Sphere and Cylinder: a sphere has two-thirds the volume and two-thirds the surface of the cylinder that just holds it. Archimedes was so proud of this that, according to Cicero, a sphere in a cylinder was carved on his tomb; Cicero found the overgrown tomb in 75 BC.
Quadrature of the Parabola: a slice of a parabola is $\tfrac43$ of the triangle inside it, found by adding up an endless series of triangles: $1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \dots = \tfrac43$.

The Sand-Reckoner: a way to name huge numbers, used to show that even the grains of sand needed to fill the universe can be counted. It also preserves the only surviving report of Aristarchus's idea that the Earth goes around the Sun.
On Spirals, On Conoids and Spheroids, and The Method, which explains how he found results by imagining shapes balanced on a lever before proving them.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: the law of the lever and Archimedes' principle, unchanged, in every physics book.
Extended: his method of adding up thin slices and endless series points straight toward the integral calculus of Newton and Leibniz.
Changed: we now compute $\pi$ by series, not polygons, to trillions of digits. But 3 10/71 < π < 3 1/7 is still correct.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: The lost book found under a prayer book

blocks.html: The Method was lost for centuries. In 1906 the Danish scholar J. L. Heiberg found it in Constantinople, in a prayer book whose parchment had been scraped and reused in the 1200s: beneath the prayers lay a copy of Archimedes from the 900s. This book, the Archimedes Palimpsest, was imaged with ultraviolet and X-ray light from 1999 to 2008, and more of Archimedes' text came back. Heath's 1912 supplement translated The Method soon after Heiberg's find.

The Method shows Archimedes' private way of discovery. He imagined a shape as made of countless thin slices and balanced them, slice by slice, against a known shape on a lever. He says plainly that this only suggests the answer, and that a proper proof must follow. The distinction he draws, between finding a result and proving it, is one later scientists kept returning to.

Ancient historians (Polybius, Livy, Plutarch) say Archimedes designed catapults and cranes that held off the Roman siege for many months. The later story that he set ships on fire with mirrors first appears centuries afterward, and modern tests have not shown it would work in battle. Plutarch also says Archimedes thought little of his machines compared with pure mathematics; that is Plutarch's view, and Archimedes' own books do take up practical questions such as floating.

items: Is guessing an answer first, then proving it, a fair way to do mathematics?
Archimedes counted the grains of sand needed to fill the universe. Why might it matter to show that a number is finite even when it is too big to write out?
Which matters more, a clever machine or a clever proof?

blocks.html: Galileo, later on this ladder, admired Archimedes above the other ancient mathematicians and built on his statics and floating bodies. Newton's calculus finished the work Archimedes' slices began.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Where do you use a lever at home? (Scissors, a bottle opener, a wheelbarrow, a door handle.) Where is the pivot on each?
  2. Why does a huge steel ship float, but a small steel nail sinks?
  3. The Eureka story may not be true. Does a good story help people remember science, or does it get in the way?
  4. Archimedes trapped π between two numbers instead of finding it exactly. When is an answer that says "between this and that" good enough?
  5. Archimedes asked for a sphere and cylinder on his tomb. If you could carve one idea you are proud of, what would it be?
